node.label: Franca Iacovetta
node.date_label: Such Hardworking People (1992) · Enemies Within (co-edited with Roberto Perin and Angelo Principe) (2000) · Gatekeepers (2006)
node.description: A Canadian historian of gender, migration and class. Gatekeepers examines how everyday institutions tried to reshape newcomers in Cold War Canada, as characterized by Basok and Bastable’s review. Her own 2019 article separately examines women’s activism and negotiated cultural assertions in mediated social-work files, with uneven power and unknown outcomes. Her editorial collaborations retain their joint credit.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Such Hardworking People (1992); Enemies Within (co-edited with Roberto Perin and Angelo Principe) (2000); Gatekeepers (2006). “Writing Women’s Community-based Pluralism into the History of Canadian Multiculturalism” (2019; selected pp. 29–32 and 35–42 read).
node.scope_note: Selected substantive passages and bibliographic records only; complete monographs not read. Existing profile/field prose, collective relationships and earlier verification qualifications remain unchanged. Citation counts selected the research queue; they do not prove importance or influence. Life status is separately documented in this local person folder; no lifespan or career interval is inferred. Gatekeepers is characterized through Basok/Bastable pp. 211–213 only for institutional gatekeeping. Claims about negotiation and gender/family ideals draw on Iacovetta’s own 2019 article, selected pp. 29–32 and 35–42, not the review’s treatment of another author. These social-work case files are mediated, outcomes are often unknown, and the Institute mainly served European newcomers; no universal account or complete monograph reading is asserted.

incident_edges.relationship: Examines everyday gatekeeping and the contested remaking of immigrant citizenship in Cold War Canada.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Correction 2026-10-25: Basok/Bastable pp. 211–213 support the gatekeeping/citizenship claim. Immigrant cultural negotiation and resistance are independently supported by Iacovetta’s own 2019 article, pp. 29–30 and 35; the review’s resistance contrast on p. 217 is preserved and is not reversed. No full-book reading.

incident_edges.relationship: Places contradictory expectations about marriage, gender and family inside immigrant social-work encounters.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Correction 2026-10-25: Iacovetta’s own 2019 article, especially pp. 39–42, analyzes male-breadwinner/female-homemaker and egalitarian marital ideals, domestic-abuse counselling, female clients’ practical negotiations, and the limits of mediated case files. This replaces the earlier attribution to the joint review’s discussion of another author; it is a scoped article reading, not full-book verification.

incident_edges.relationship: With Linda Kealey, Iacovetta answers Sangster’s Beyond Dichotomies, objecting that its polemic risks oversimplification and misrepresentation while welcoming debate (1996).
incident_edges.evidence_note: The opening expressly names Sangster’s essay and frames the response as disagreement among friends and colleagues. Linda Kealey is coauthor; she is not Gregory S.Kealey. Do not treat this as a single-author reply.

incident_edges.relationship: Replying to Iacovetta and Linda Kealey, Sangster welcomes their review but contests the simplification charge and treats gender as both standpoint and field (1996).
incident_edges.evidence_note: This is a qualified rejoinder: p. 247 stresses shared questions and theoretical overlap. It must not turn Iacovetta/Kealey into simple poststructuralist adversaries or erase the coauthor.

named_group_routes.relationship: Canadian debates over gender as a category
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Pierson's 1991 essay opens on feminist historians' turn to deconstruction and discourse analysis, naming Scott's theory of gender as the most acclaimed example. Parr (1995) and the 1995–96 Left History exchange (Sangster; Iacovetta and Kealey; Dubinsky and Marks) argued over gender history and women's history; their citations are checked, and Sangster's own position is taken from her 2011 retrospect; the replies are read only as defences of gender history. PhD context: 64 of 328 PhDs engaging this group cite Scott (20% vs 9% of all; lift 2.12).

named_group_routes.relationship: Gender and class as simultaneous hierarchies, and gender history as a practice in Canadian women's history (1985–96)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985, read in full): women and children are not tied together as subjects by nature; 'What distinguishes feminine and preschooler from masculine and prime of life is not naturalness versus artificiality but proximity to power' (p. 39). She criticises the mid-1970s Canadian literature on reform for characterising 1880–1920 as 'an era of "maternal feminism"', seeing women's public actions 'definitionally as an extension of the private' (p. 41), and asks historians to 'stop shying away from the word "patriarchy"' and to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict' (p. 44). She presents this as a change 'a good many others have already begun to suggest' (p. 39). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), unread here, as reviewers quote it: Guildford (Atlantis, 1991, p. 140) says she rejects 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' (p. 8) and argues 'that class and gender are made and experienced simultaneously'; Bertaux (JEH, 1992, p. 241) quotes p. 9 on 'these galloping pairs—class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. Reception in the Left History exchange (all read in full): Sangster calls the book 'One of the path breaking books on gender history' (1995, p. 120); Iacovetta and Kealey call her 'recognized as a leading practitioner of gender history' (1996, p. 222) and 'a major figure in the field', quoting her 1995 CHR essay (pp. 362–63) that 'gender history made masculinity and femininity commensurably problematical historically, while insisting that neither could be well understood without companion inquiries into the other hierarchies with which they were mutually intertwined' (p. 228); Dubinsky and Marks cite her for refraining 'from imposing one category - be it class or gender - on historical actors' (1996, p. 211). Criticism: Sangster (1996, p. 240 n. 2) characterises Parr's essay (its reprint in Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11, unread here) as placing critics 'feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group' (Sangster's wording, not a quotation from Parr), notes that she had been reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr' (p. 240 n. 3), and, quoting Parr's line that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships' (reprint p. 14), questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (pp. 244, 246). The 1995 essay itself is unread: its words here are quoted by Iacovetta and Kealey and by Sangster. Not a founding: the field's gender debate also runs through Pierson (1991) and Scott (edge_891). Later reading, labelled: a 2026 CHR 'great books' forum (abstract only) calls the book 'a path-breaking study that challenged established dichotomies in social theory'.

named_group_routes.relationship: Her two-town study (1990) and 1995 essay deconstructed skill and treated 'portraits of experience' as 'interpretations, reclamations of sensations', while keeping 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy' (as read by Sangster, 2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Both Parr texts are unread (the existing Parr entry records the 1995 essay as known only through Iacovetta–Kealey and Sangster). Sangster 2000, read in full: the 'polar worlds of men's and women's work in small town Ontario' show 'the positive results of talking gender' (p. 151, citing The Gender of Breadwinners); Parr grouped with Tillotson, Mercedes Steedman and Creese as having 'deconstructed the notion of skill' while 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy are still in evidence, unlike the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (p. 157); from the 1995 essay (p. 364) the sentence that portraits of experience 'were interpretations, reclamations of sensations which first had been organized, then claimed as experience' (p. 159, as quoted by Sangster). Moderate: a named reader's account.

sources.title: Tanya Basok and Marshall Bastable, “Knock, Knock, Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door”, Labour/Le Travail 63 (2009), 207–219

verification.note: Complete review essay read; Iacovetta discussion especially 209–214. Reviewers analyze surveillance, liberal citizenship, gender/family and immigrant accommodation/resistance, and question the scope of exclusion. Other books in this joint review are not attributed to Iacovetta. Correction 2026-10-25: The earlier complete-reading claim and attribution were overstated. The Iacovetta-specific discussion is on pp. 211–213 and concerns Cold War gatekeeping, citizenship and bourgeois cultural norms; p. 217 explicitly contrasts Goutor/Iacovetta with Zaman on resistance. The detailed gender/family and resistance discussion of Zaman must not be attributed to Iacovetta. Iacovetta’s own 2019 article, now added as hc178_iacovetta_primary_2019, independently supports gender/family regulation and immigrant negotiation. The review remains a named substantive reader for the narrower gatekeeping claim; no complete monograph reading is asserted.

sources.citation: Joy Parr, “Nature and Hierarchy: Reflections on Writing the History of Women and Children,” Atlantis 11, no. 1 (Fall 1985): 39–44.

verification.note: Read in full in the journal's PDF (article/download/4974/4172); citation metadata from the article page (vol. 11, no. 1, 1985, pp. 39–44). Pages assigned by PDF order (p. 42 is printed). Passages used: 'Is it nature which ties women and children together as subjects? Clearly not'; 'proximity to power'; 'a good many others have already begun to suggest' (p. 39); 'an era of "maternal feminism"' (p. 41); 'students of men's work and men's participation in labour organisations, have reified the skill-unskill boundary' (p. 42); 'Skill, too, is a socially constructed category' (pp. 42–43); Women at Work (1975) and the Marxist analysis that 'tells us nothing about why women end up at the bottom of this hierarchy', quoted from feminist critics (n. 20: Phillips and Taylor; Hartmann) (p. 43); 'stop shying away from the word "patriarchy"'; 'gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict' (p. 44).

sources.scope_note: Her own in-period statement of gender and class as simultaneous hierarchies, and of women and children as a subject defined by power.

sources.title: Joan W. Scott: Gender as a category of historical analysis
sources.citation: Joan W. Scott, “Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis,” American Historical Review 91, no. 5 (1986): 1053–75, especially 1059–60.

verification.note: Scanned pages 1059–60 checked for Marxist feminist approaches, British socialist-feminist debates, and Scott’s criticism of economic determination. This is her intervention, not a consensus account of all gender history. Additional primary pp. 1067–1068 checked in revision 1.25: Rosaldo and Foucault named, gender defined relationally, institutions and subjective identity distinguished, and universal psychoanalytic claims qualified. Full article remains unreviewed. Additional 2026-09-12 reading: complete printed pp. 1062–1066 through OCR of PDF indices 10–14. Scott finds constructed subjectivity instructive but criticizes universal binary antagonism and insufficient historical variability; she discusses Sally Alexander, de Lauretis and Riley and productively cites Derrida. These are Scott’s readings, not independent readings of every cited work. Original cited Lacanian collections and Alexander essay remain uncollated. Addendum 2026-10-17: Revision 1.143: printed p. 1054 read (OCR of the same scan). Those who wanted ‘a relational notion’ used ‘gender’; ‘Thus Natalie Davis suggested in 1975, “It seems to me that we should be interested in the history of both women and men … Our goal is to understand the significance of the sexes, of gender groups in the historical past …”’ (n. 4: Feminist Studies 3, Winter 1975–76, p. 90). Davis’s words are as Scott quotes them.

sources.title: Joan Sangster, “Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History: Exploring the Past, Present and Future,” Labour/Le Travail 46 (2000): 127ff.
sources.citation: Joan Sangster, “Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History: Exploring the Past, Present and Future,” Labour/Le Travail 46 (2000): 127ff.

verification.note: Abstract read: thirty years of women’s labour history shaped by feminist, left and labour organizing, international social theory and Canadian historiography; feminist challenges to the initially ‘masculinist’ shape of working-class history, and calls to integrate race and ethnicity, shifted its narrative and paradigms; gender more effectively though not completely integrated into class formation; post-structuralism and the decline of the left unsettle the field. Checked against: Crossref DOI record; OpenAlex abstract (English and French). Addendum 2026-10-14: Read at pp. 130 and 133 and searched for Kealey in the journal's PDF (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/5205) for the 1.138 Kealey draft. p. 130 n. 8: Kealey (1995, p. 125) on two overlapping cohorts of the 1960s and 1970s; p. 133: 'One of the first major collections of the new labour history contained not one article on women' (Kealey and Warrian, Essays, 1976); 'Two seminal studies followed by Gregory Kealey and Bryan Palmer. Though differently positioned politically, they examined workers' responses to 19th century industrialization, with a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere'.
